content: Rabies is an almost universally fatal disease, with tens of thousands of deaths reported annually and only a few documented survivors. Globally, an estimated 59,000 people die from suspected or confirmed rabies each year, with the majority of these deaths occurring in poor, rural communities in Asia and Africa. Most patients initially seek care in peripheral or village health centers, where resources for basic wound care and rabies prevention are often inadequate or absent. Once clinical signs of rabies appear, there is no effective curative treatment, and nearly all patients succumb to the disease. Management of rabies patients focuses on palliative care, as aggressive treatment options are rarely effective. Patients with rabies often remain conscious and aware of their condition, which can lead to significant agitation, particularly in cases of furious rabies. Isolation is commonly practiced to minimize perceived risks of transmission, although human-to-human transmission is extremely rare. In some countries, patients are turned away from hospitals and receive terminal care only from their families. Hospital care, when available, is recommended to reduce suffering and provide respectful, culturally sensitive palliative care. Palliative care for rabies patients should prioritize comfort, with heavy sedation (e.g. Sedatives like diazepam, lorazepam, or midazolam can be administered subcutaneously, intravenously, or rectally to manage agitation and muscle spasms. Morphine may be used for pain relief, though it is often difficult to access in resource-limited settings. Anticholinergic agents, such as scopolamine, can help manage excessive salivation. Drugs should be carefully titrated to avoid excessive sedation that might necessitate intubation. Health care providers play a critical role in delivering holistic, compassionate, and culturally sensitive care, even in settings with limited resources. Families should be informed about the patient’s condition and prognosis as early as possible. Emotional and physical support should be provided in a calm, quiet environment that respects the patient’s dignity and cultural needs. The family’s ability to communicate with the patient during their final moments should be preserved. Aggressive treatment protocols, such as the Milwaukee protocol, have been attempted in rare cases but have not consistently resulted in survival without severe neurological sequelae. Survivors of rabies are extremely rare, and most have received at least one dose of rabies vaccine before the onset of symptoms. Aggressive management should only be considered in specialized centers with experienced teams and after ruling out other treatable conditions. Ethical considerations and discussions with the patient’s family are essential before pursuing such approaches. Rabies-specific treatment research is ongoing, including the development of antiviral agents and strategies to enhance drug delivery across the blood-brain barrier. However, these treatments must be proven safe and effective before clinical use. Salvage treatment protocols should be ethically approved before implementation. The bodies of patients who have died from rabies should be handled with standard precautions, as the risk of transmission is extremely low. Blood does not contain the rabies virus, but the virus is present in other tissues and fluids, such as the central nervous system and salivary glands. Burial or cremation should be conducted according to the deceased’s religious practices. Organ transplantation from individuals who have died with neurological symptoms suggestive of rabies should be approached with caution. Rabies transmission through organ and tissue transplantation has been documented, and testing for fatal infections should be balanced against the urgency of transplantation. The World Health Organization (WHO) strongly recommends discontinuing the use of nerve tissue vaccines due to their severe adverse effects and lower immunogenicity compared to CCEEVs. Vaccines must meet international standards of quality and good manufacturing practices. Currently, three rabies vaccines are prequalified for intramuscular use: purified Vero cell rabies vaccine, purified chick embryo cell vaccine, and purified duck embryo vaccine. In summary, rabies remains a devastating disease with limited treatment options once symptoms appear. Palliative care should be an integral part of rabies management guidelines, ensuring that patients receive compassionate and respectful care during their final stages.
